title: What is CI/CD?
description: Continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment — what each term means, the pipeline stages, and why fast feedback beats big-bang releases.

data.text: **Continuous Integration** means developers merge small changes frequently, and every merge automatically builds and tests the code so breakage is found in minutes, not weeks. **Continuous Delivery** extends that: every green build is packaged and kept ready to release to production at any time (with a human click). **Continuous Deployment** goes one step further — green builds go to production automatically. The pipeline is the machine that makes this repeatable: build → test → package → deploy, with the same artifact promoted through environments.

**Why it works:** small, frequent merges minimize merge conflicts and shrink the search space for bugs (the last green commit is one change away). Big-bang integration — merging everyone's month of work before release week — produces 'integration hell' where one failure blocks everything.

**Typical pipeline stages:**
1. **Build** — restore, compile; fail fast on compile errors
2. **Test** — unit tests, then integration tests; the artifact from this stage is *the* release candidate, not rebuilt later
3. **Package** — Docker image or NuGet/npm package with an immutable version/tag
4. **Deploy** — dev → test → staging, with smoke checks; production next (manual gate for delivery, automatic for deployment)
5. **Verify** — health checks, canary metrics, alerting on SLOs

**Supporting practices:** trunk-based development or short-lived branches, test automation (manual QA gates kill pipeline speed), infrastructure as code so environments are reproducible, and secrets managed by the pipeline's identity, not checked-in config.

**Failure modes to name:** flaky tests (people start re-running instead of fixing, eroding trust), pipelines over 10–15 minutes (developers batch changes again), and deploying the *source* instead of promoting one immutable artifact through all environments.

data.title: A minimal GitHub Actions pipeline
data.code:
name: build-test-deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: '9.0.x' }
      - run: dotnet restore
      - run: dotnet build --no-restore
      - run: dotnet test --no-build --logger trx        # gate: all green
      - run: docker build -t myapi:${{ github.sha }} .  # one immutable artifact
      - run: docker push registry/myapi:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: az aks kubectl ... apply image tag ${{ github.sha }}
      # smoke tests here; production deploy = same tag, different environment
      # (delivery: manual gate; deployment: automatic)

data.text: Quick recall: CI = integrate + test frequently; delivery = always releasable; deployment = auto-release. Bonus: pipeline stages and one supporting practice (short branches, artifact promotion, test automation).

items: Using CI, CD, and 'deployment' interchangeably without distinguishing them
Rebuilding the artifact for production instead of promoting one immutable build
Ignoring flaky tests — they're pipeline debt that trains people to re-run
Leaving the deploy step manual all the way to prod and calling it continuous
How do you handle database migrations in a CI/CD pipeline?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CI: frequent merges, automatic build+test feedback in minutes
Continuous delivery: every green build is releasable
Continuous deployment: green builds release automatically
Promote one immutable artifact through environments; fix flaky tests fast
data.takeaway: CI/CD is a feedback machine: the shorter the merge-to-verified-commit loop, the cheaper every bug is to fix.
